headings.title: Introduction to Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) and Medicalisation
headings.content: Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) encompasses all procedures involving the partial or total removal of the external female genitalia or other injury to the female genital organs for non-medical reasons. Traditionally performed by traditional practitioners, there has been a concerning shift towards the medicalisation of FGM. Medicalised FGM refers to situations where FGM is practiced by any health care provider—whether a doctor, nurse, midwife, or other trained medical personnel—either in public or private health facilities. This trend represents a profound violation of fundamental human rights, medical ethics, and professional nursing standards. For nursing students in Nigeria and across Africa, understanding this phenomenon is critical because health professionals are uniquely positioned to either perpetuate or eradicate the practice. Medicalisation often gives a false sense of safety and legitimacy to a harmful cultural practice, leading communities to believe that having a trained nurse or doctor perform the procedure minimizes health risks. However, international bodies like the World Health Organization (WHO) explicitly condemn the medicalisation of FGM, emphasizing that no medical professional should ever perform it under any circumstances. Nursing education must address this topic head-on, equipping students with the knowledge to recognize, resist, and report attempts to medicalise FGM within healthcare systems.

headings.title: Understanding the Concept and Drivers of Medicalised FGM
headings.content: To effectively combat the medicalisation of FGM, student nurses must understand the underlying drivers and socio-cultural concepts that fuel the practice. FGM is deeply rooted in gender inequality, patriarchal control, and deeply ingrained social norms regarding female chastity, modesty, and marriageability. When families seek out medicalised FGM, their primary motivation is often the misconception that involving a trained clinician will eliminate or significantly reduce the risk of severe physical complications, such as haemorrhage or fatal sepsis. Some healthcare providers themselves succumb to these pressures, driven by financial incentives, cultural pressure from their own communities, or misguided attempts at 'harm reduction'—the false belief that performing a milder form of the procedure or using local anesthesia is a compassionate compromise. However, public health research clearly shows that medicalisation does not eliminate the psychological, sexual, and long-term obstetric complications associated with FGM. Furthermore, participating in medicalised FGM compromises patient trust and breaches the sacred oath of non-maleficence ('do no harm'). Recognizing these complex socio-cultural and economic drivers enables nurses to engage communities with empathy while standing firm against any clinical involvement.

headings.title: Types of Procedures Performed in Clinical Settings
headings.content: FGM is classified into four main types by the World Health Organization, and all of these variants can unfortunately be encountered in clinical settings where medicalisation occurs. Type I involves the partial or total removal of the clitoris and/or the prepuce (clitoridectomy). Type II involves the partial or total removal of the clitoris and the labia minora, with or without excision of the labia majora. Type III, commonly known as infibulation, involves the narrowing of the vaginal orifice through the creation of a covering seal formed by cutting and positioning the labia minora or majora, with or without excision of the clitoris. Type IV includes all other harmful procedures to the female genitalia for non-medical purposes, such as pricking, piercing, incising, scraping, and cauterization. When performed in clinical settings, healthcare workers might use surgical blades, local anesthetics, and sutures, creating a sterile illusion of a surgical operation. This clinical framing misleads patients and families into treating an act of mutilation as a routine medical procedure. Nurses must be familiar with these classifications to accurately assess patients, document findings during physical examinations, and provide appropriate holistic care to survivors seeking medical or psychological support.

headings.title: Public Health Implications and Complications
headings.content: Regardless of whether FGM is performed by a traditional practitioner with a rusty blade or a trained nurse with sterile instruments, the procedure carries severe, debilitating public health consequences. Immediate complications include severe pain, haemorrhage, shock, acute urinary retention, and overwhelming infections such as tetanus. Long-term physical complications are equally devastating, affecting women throughout their lifespan. These include chronic pelvic pain, recurrent urinary tract infections, formation of dermoid cysts, painful sexual intercourse (dyspareunia), and psychological trauma such as anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Obstetric complications are a major burden in regions with high FGM prevalence; women with infibulated scars frequently experience prolonged obstructed labor, increased rates of obstetric fistula, severe perineal tearing, and elevated risks of perinatal and maternal mortality. The medicalisation of FGM does not prevent these lifelong consequences, because the anatomical and physiological destruction of healthy genital tissue inherently disrupts normal bodily functions. As future public health nurses, students must understand these complications to provide evidence-based care, advocate for survivors, and educate communities on the inescapable health hazards of the practice.

headings.title: Ethical, Legal, and Professional Frameworks for Nurses
headings.content: Nurses and midwives operate within strict ethical, legal, and professional frameworks that categorically prohibit participation in FGM or its medicalisation. Ethically, the core nursing principles of beneficence (acting in the patient's best interest) and non-maleficence (doing no harm) are directly violated by performing or condoning FGM. Legally, many countries—including Nigeria, through the Violence Against Persons Prohibition (VAPP) Act—have enacted robust legislation criminalising FGM in all its forms, explicitly penalizing health workers who partake in medicalised FGM with fines, imprisonment, and revocation of their professional licenses. Professional regulatory bodies, such as the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN), view medicalised FGM as professional misconduct and gross negligence. Nurses have a professional and moral duty not only to refuse participation but also to report colleagues or facilities engaging in the practice. Understanding these legal and ethical boundaries protects nursing students and practicing professionals from legal liability and reinforces the integrity of the nursing profession as a guardian of public health and human rights.

headings.title: Community Health Nursing Strategies for Prevention and Advocacy
headings.content: Community health nursing strategies are vital in the multi-sectoral effort to eradicate FGM and its medicalisation. Nurses serve as educators, advocates, and change agents at the grassroots level. Effective community health interventions require culturally sensitive, non-judgmental approaches that engage key community stakeholders, including traditional rulers, religious leaders, mothers, and traditional circumcisers. Rather than merely condemning communities, nurses must facilitate open, participatory dialogues that explore the health consequences of FGM and debunk the myths surrounding medicalisation. Economic empowerment programs and alternative rites of passage that celebrate coming-of-age without genital cutting are powerful community-based strategies supported by public health nurses. Furthermore, nurses must establish supportive, confidential environments in primary healthcare centers so that survivors can access psychological counseling, management of chronic complications, and empathetic maternity care. By combining community education, policy enforcement, and compassionate clinical care, community health nurses play a pivotal role in shifting social norms and protecting future generations of girls from both traditional and medicalised FGM.
